title: The Strange Education Legacy of 9/11 September 17, 2026
author: Dale Chu
source: Thomas B. Fordham Institute, Flypaper (fordhaminstitute.org), September 11, 2026,
summary: On the 25th anniversary of September 11, former third-grade teacher Dale Chu reflects on how the attacks shaped American education policy in ways that now contrast sharply with the response to Covid. He recalls that President Bush was at a Florida elementary school promoting No Child Left Behind that morning, and argues that the crisis created a political moment that pushed the stalled bipartisan law across the finish line. Chu separates NCLB's flaws, especially its utopian 100 percent proficiency target, from its animating principle that schools should not hide disadvantaged students' performance behind averages, and points to substantial NAEP gains for Black and Hispanic students through the early 2010s. Drawing on NCLB architect Sandy Kress, he then makes the paradoxical move that 9/11 also dissolved the reform coalition by redirecting national attention to security and restoring partisan politics, leading to ESSA and stalled achievement. The pandemic, by contrast, deepened divisions instead of uniting the country, and Chu argues prolonged school closures turned a plateau into a steep decline, leaving millions of children further behind.
points: The 9/11 attacks created the bipartisan urgency that pushed No Child Left Behind into law after negotiations between the White House and congressional Democrats had stalled.
Chu distinguishes NCLB's compliance-driven 100 percent proficiency target from its lasting principle of annual testing, disaggregated results, and accountability for disadvantaged students.
According to Sandy Kress, 9/11 also unraveled the reform coalition as attention shifted to Afghanistan and Al Qaeda and normal partisan politics returned.
NAEP reading scores for Hispanic and Black fourth graders rose 20 and 21 points during the reform era before stalling in the mid-2010s, especially for the lowest performers.
Whereas one national crisis united policymakers around student outcomes, Covid split them, and Chu argues schools should have been among the first institutions reopened.
quotes: It’s easy to forget that, on the morning of September 11, 2001, President George W. Bush was literally at an elementary school in Florida promoting No Child Left Behind.

The law’s utopian 100 percent proficiency target in reading and math flattened a worthy goal into a bureaucratic compliance exercise. However, these shortcomings should be separated from the law’s animating principle: Schools and districts shouldn’t be permitted to hide the performance of disadvantaged children behind averages.
The attacks redirected the country’s attention toward national security and foreign policy, and although they initially forged a rare sense of national unity, partisan politics gradually returned.

But instead of bringing Americans together, it exacerbated existing divisions. Education was a particularly vivid example: Debates over masks, social distancing, testing, vaccines, remote instruction, and extended school closures quickly became partisan and institutional battles.
Whatever one’s views about the broader pandemic response, schools should have been among the first institutions we fought to restore because our children had so much to lose.

The strange education legacy of 9/11 was, in many ways, an accident of history. The attacks helped propel an ambitious national education agenda into law, even as the political coalition behind it eventually unraveled.
